sections.h2: How is property valued and taxed in Minnesota?
sections.html:
Minnesota lists real property by its January 2 value, and assessors must look at a fifth of all parcels each year, which puts every parcel on a five year maximum cycle (Minn. Stat. 273.01). The standard is market value. Minn. Stat. 273.11 tells the assessor to value property at its market value and bars a lower standard just because the figure will serve as a tax base, or a forced-sale price as the benchmark.

Every owner of record gets a mailed valuation notice at least ten days before the local appeal board convenes (Minn. Stat. 273.121). It states two years of market value and classification, the assessor's address, and the meeting dates for the local board and the county board. An owner who never receives it still owes the tax, since a missed notice does not undo the assessment.

sections.h2: What are the two Minnesota payment dates and the late charges?
sections.html:
A parcel taxed over $100 pays in halves, the first before May 16 and the second before October 16 (Minn. Stat. 279.01). Missing a due date adds two percent for homestead and four percent for nonhomestead property. If any balance remains once the next month begins, another two or four percent is added. After that, each month through December adds one percent, up to a ceiling of eight percent for homestead and 12 percent for nonhomestead.

  • If the statement was not postmarked before April 25, the first-half date moves to 21 days after the postmark.
  • Taxes of $100 or less are due in full on the first-half date.
  • The treasurer can accept an amount above or below the installment and credits it to the oldest balance first.
  • A payment postmarked within one business day after the deadline earns a one-time penalty waiver.
  • Farm homestead owners have until November 15 for the second half.

The county also mails a notice of proposed property taxes after November 10 and on or before November 24 each year (Minn. Stat. 275.065). It lists the market value, the current tax and the proposed tax for the next year, and the time and place of the budget meetings. Those public meetings take place after November 24 and not before 6:00 p.m.

sections.h2: What steps lead to a lower Minnesota assessment?
sections.html:
There are three stages, and skipping the first can limit the second. The local board of appeal and equalization meets between April 1 and May 31 under Minn. Stat. 274.01, and clerks must post and publish notice at least ten days ahead. The board reviews the assessment or classification of any property owner who feels aggrieved. It may reduce assessments on petition, but total reductions cannot lower the assessor's aggregate by more than one percent, and the board cannot grant an exemption or remove property from the rolls.

An owner who was warned of a proposed increase and then ignores the hearing, or who never asks for review at all, generally loses the right to go before the county board. The exception covers an owner who did not get notice of the market value five days or more ahead of the local session. Local boards have 20 days to wrap up unless the revenue commissioner allows longer.

The county board of appeal and equalization meets after the second Friday in June, can sit up to ten meeting days, and its actions after June 30 are invalid except for permitted corrections (Minn. Stat. 274.14). At least one meeting day must run until at least 7:00 p.m. or offer evening appointments. The last stop is court. Under Minn. Stat. 278.01, an owner can petition district court or Tax Court by serving a copy on the county auditor and filing proof of service with the court administrator by April 30 of the payable year. A change notice that first reaches the owner after February 28 starts a 60 day window counted from the date it was mailed.

sections.html:

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Minnesota property tax when a house is sold?
sections.html:
The county auditor checks the records for delinquent taxes before it transfers land on the books. Minn. Stat. 272.12 says that when a deed is presented, the auditor certifies any delinquent taxes, and once they are paid or none exist the deed is marked "no delinquent taxes and transfer entered." Without that notation the recorder or registrar of titles must refuse to record most deeds. Deeds of distribution in probate, foreclosure certificates and a few other instruments follow separate wording.

Taxes that stay unpaid can eventually lead to forfeiture. Minn. Stat. 281.17 sets the redemption period for land sold to the state at a tax judgment sale at three years from the date of the sale to the state. It drops to one year for land in a targeted community, except for homesteaded lands, and for a qualified mixed municipal solid waste disposal facility. The county uses the classification that applied in the assessment year of the tax judgment.

Special assessments for local improvements run on a separate track. Under Minn. Stat. 429.061, the city council holds a hearing after mailing each owner a notice that states the amount assessed, the right to prepay and the interest rate. An appeal over the amount requires a written objection filed with the clerk before or at the hearing, and an appeal to district court through service on the mayor or clerk within 30 days after adoption. The court petition process in section 278.01 is not available for special assessments.

sections.h2: What relief programs lower a Minnesota property tax bill?
sections.html:
Several programs apply by statute, each with its own application. The right one depends on whether the problem is value, income or timing.

  • Homestead classification, with a market value exclusion that starts at 40 percent for homes valued at $95,000 or less, is described in Minn. Stat. 273.13, subdivision 35.
  • The homestead credit refund in Minn. Stat. 290A.04 pays up to $3,310 and ends at household income of $135,410.
  • The senior deferral in Minn. Stat. 290B.03 allows qualifying owners 65 and older with household income of $96,000 or less to defer taxes.
  • County abatement under Minn. Stat. 375.192 can reduce value, taxes, penalties or interest on written application, within limits for earlier years.
  • Owners on federal active service as members of the National Guard or a reserve component get a four-month grace period on homestead tax due dates, with orders attached to the payment.

Owners who inherit a house or buy one should check classification first. If the county classified a property as nonhomestead and the owner qualifies, a written application to the county board under section 375.192 may correct it.

faqs.q: What dates do Minnesota property tax installments fall on?
faqs.a: Half before May 16 and half before October 16 when the tax is above $100. Taxes of $100 or less are due in full with the first half. If the statement was mailed late, the first half date moves to 21 days after the postmark.

faqs.q: What is the penalty for paying Minnesota property tax late?
faqs.a: Two percent on homestead and four percent on nonhomestead property on the due date, the same again if a balance remains into the next month, then one percent a month through December. The total stops at eight percent for homestead and 12 percent for nonhomestead.

faqs.q: Where do I start if my Minnesota valuation looks too high?
faqs.a: Begin with the town or city board in April or May, move to the county board in June if needed, and use a court petition as the last step, filed by April 30 of the payable year. Special assessments follow their own objection route.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Minnesota house that has delinquent property taxes?
faqs.a: Yes, once the delinquent taxes are paid. The county auditor certifies them when the deed is presented, and the deed is not marked for recording until then. Phone the treasurer's office for a written payoff figure before closing.

faqs.q: What is the redemption window after a Minnesota tax judgment sale?
faqs.a: Generally three years from the date the land was sold to the state. It is one year for land in a targeted community, except homesteaded land, and for certain solid waste disposal facilities.
